selected.hypothesis: Electrides can be identified by (a) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (b) a very low minimum Pauling electronegativity, (c) a large spread of electronegativities that creates strong donor‑acceptor contrast, (d) a large maximum interstitial clearance, (e) a positive mean clearance indicating overall spaciousness, (f) a substantial metallic site fraction providing a conductive backbone, and (g) a low total_assignment_count reflecting few charge‑balanced oxidation‑state solutions and thus excess electrons.

final_fit.note: Model fitted on all labeled structures; probability >= 0.5 means electride. Missing feature values are imputed with the median of these structures.

leaderboard.hypothesis: Electrides can be identified by (a) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (b) a very low minimum Pauling electronegativity, (c) a large spread of electronegativities that creates strong donor‑acceptor contrast, (d) a large maximum interstitial clearance, (e) a positive mean clearance indicating overall spaciousness, (f) a substantial metallic site fraction providing a conductive backbone, and (g) a low total_assignment_count reflecting few charge‑balanced oxidation‑state solutions and thus excess electrons.

Electrides can be identified by (a) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (b) a very low minimum Pauling electronegativity, (c) a large spread (standard deviation) of electronegativities that creates strong donor‑acceptor contrast, (d) a large maximum cavity clearance, (e) a positive mean clearance indicating overall spaciousness, (f) heterogeneity of cavity size (clearance std), and (g) a substantial metallic site fraction that supplies a conductive framework for delocalised interstitial electrons.

Electrides are identified by a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, a large spread of electronegativities indicating strong donor‑acceptor contrast, spacious and heterogeneous interstitial voids, a high volume per atom reflecting cage‑like frameworks, low transition‑metal and f‑block content, and a high count of possible oxidation‑state assignments that signals excess electrons.

Electrides can be identified by (i) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (ii) a low minimum Pauling electronegativity, (iii) large interstitial voids measured by both maximum and average sampled clearance, (iv) a metallic framework indicated by metal_site_fraction, and (v) cavity‑size heterogeneity captured by the clearance standard deviation.

Electrides are distinguished by (a) a high proportion of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (b) a large spread of elemental electronegativities that creates strong donor‑acceptor contrast, (c) overall spacious interstitial space (positive mean clearance), (d) an open lattice (high volume per atom), (e) a metallic framework that can stabilise delocalised electrons, (f) a limited set of charge‑balanced oxidation‑state assignments (low total_assignment_count) indicating excess electrons, and (g) many accessible void‑center candidates (high candidate_count_before_output_limit).

Electrides are identified by (1) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth cations, (2) low minimum Pauling electronegativity, (3) the absence of a neutral oxidation‑state assignment (excess electrons), (4) large and uniformly sized interstitial voids, and (5) low fractions of transition‑metal and f‑block sites that would otherwise bind electrons.

Electrides combine a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites with a very low minimum electronegativity, exhibit a pronounced spread of electronegativities, possess sufficiently large interstitial clearances and overall spacious lattices, have few viable charge‑balanced oxidation‑state assignments, and avoid f‑block elements.

Electrides are distinguished by (a) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (b) a very low minimum Pauling electronegativity indicating strongly reducing cations, (c) a large maximum interstitial clearance that can host anionic electrons, (d) overall spacious lattices (high volume per atom), (e) few charge‑balanced oxidation‑state assignments (low total_assignment_count) signalling excess electrons, (f) a metallic site fraction that provides a conductive backbone, and (g) a positive mean sampled clearance reflecting generally open interstitial space.
